We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

A 3D human anatomy application built with @threejs using GPT 5.6 Sol. It all started with a single design image that I created using GPT Image 2.0. I then used it to generate every 3D organ image, one by one. Next, I converted each of those images into 3D models using @tripoai (and no, they didn't sponsor this 😄). After that, I opened Codex, wrote a master prompt based on the design, and gave it the prompt, the design image, and all the 3D models. Codex built the first version beautifully, but there was one big problem. Every single 3D model was nearly 120-150 MB. That obviously wasn't practical for the web and was giving a performance of 16fps. After a few iterations, Codex optimized each model down to roughly 2–5.5 MB while preserving the visual quality, reducing the total asset size from ~900 MB to just 28.6 MB. And each model loads on demand. Along the way, Codex also generated those anatomical illustrations showing where each organ sits in the human body, and even created the interactive hotspot markers that explain different parts of every organ. It handled all of that. The process wasn't exactly one shot, but it also wasn't difficult. You just have to do it step by step. It genuinely felt like building something that could make learning anatomy much more engaging. The inspiration came from @DilumSanjaya 's 3D animal plant cell project. People keep asking why DeepSeek’s API is so cheap. Some even make absurd claims that they’re dumping prices to corner the market. No, the answer is simple: their model size is ridiculously small compared to its performance. It's 10x smaller than Opus, and 5x smaller than Sonnet. That means what used to require an 8-chip node can now run on a single chip. And because it's so small, it runs extremely fast. You can multi-serve multiple users from a single chip while maintaining decent speeds. By my math, they can handle 40x~ more traffic than Opus using the exact same compute. This is where the competition is heading, and it’s why they can stay profitable even at these crazy prices.

If you want to join an ambitious and pragmatic AI safety team, you should get in touch :) Alex Robey (@AlexRobey23) 1/ There's not a clear one-size-fits-all formula for open-weight releases. Each release should weigh a bunch of things: dual-use capabilities, how robust safeguards are (e.g., to fine-tuning attacks), accessibility (cost/infra/etc.), and the overall ecosystem. Any future model release will need to evolve the criteria as models improve. 2/ Can dangerous and general capabilities be decoupled? Unclear in general, but likely answerable per domain. For biosecurity, filtering seems promising: harm is tied to specific empirical knowledge (protocols, conditions, etc.) that may be harder to rederive. For cyber, filtering seems harder: dangerous capability largely rides on reasoning + coding. 3/ There's a ton of research to do. One thing I'm excited about is adversarial fine-tuning as capability measurement. We know refusals can be stripped (abliteration, jailbreaks, etc.). The harder question is how one can measure worst-case capabilities, i.e., what can an adversarial user truly elicit (as a function of data/compute/effort)? — https://nitter.net/AlexRobey23/status/2083341332370878765#m

It's not time to slow down but to accelerate! The recent AI-powered cyberattacks have everyone talking about the risks of AI. We should. But let's not lose sight of the bigger picture! If we work hard at it, AI will make the world safer, not less safe, just as most major technologies have. We've already seen a glimpse of that: we defended ourselves with AI (more specifically an open model). The same systems that helped stop an AI-powered cyberattack can now help defend against millions of cyberattacks every day, while helping us identify and fix vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them. To get there, we need three things in my opinion: - Increase transparency with mandatory trace sharing and incident disclosure for agent cyber-attacks - Keep AI-powered cyberattacks illegal, with meaningful penalties to disincentivize them - Equip defenders with the best AI, especially open models, to reduce the asymmetry of capabilities between attackers and defenders If we get those three things right, AI won't just create new cybersecurity challenges, it will make cybersecurity fundamentally and meaningfully stronger. And that's before considering AI's impact on science, healthcare, education, productivity, and much more. It's not time to slow down but to accelerate!

This short course was built with @Cerebras and taught by @zhennydez , @duerr_seb , and @MilksandMatcha . When a model generates text, much of the time is spent moving its weights out of memory and into the compute units. In this course, the hardware you'll use is Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, which is designed for fast inference by keeping the model's weights close to the compute units. Adam Thierer had written the landmark book on "Permissionless Innovation." We get the best ideas when we don't have to ask the government in advance for permission to invent. Protecting open source AI is now a critical part of ensuring this. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) We stand at a critical crossroads in the debate over AI governance in the United States, and it feels like we are inching closer to a very serious battle over whether or not open source models will even be allowed in an environment where a new de facto licensing regime has been taking shape. Lacking formal congressional statutory frameworks or clear administration rules (like the diffusion rule revision), we appear to be left with a sporadic, arbitrary, non-transparent process for model review. The fiction of “voluntary” agreements hangs over this debate, and some large model developers are already showing an incredible willingness to bend over backwards to accommodate national security-related officials / orders that the rest of us are not privy to. It's a very opaque process. And those model developers are expected to play ball with those officials, or else their models get pulled from the market or held up for long periods. Or they will lose any government procurement contracts they have. There is nothing “voluntary” about it when that Sword of Damocles hangs in the room. As this mess worsens, at some point the question of how to handle open source models will come into sharper focus because it will have to. I've even heard some rumors lately that something may be coming from the admin on this front to address this. Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. If that happens, then we would be right back in the thick of a Clipper Chip-like battle along the lines of what we saw in the late 1990s. That is a much darker path for America. Meanwhile, open source developers have no “golden shares” or other goodies to offer the government to make their problems go away. Let’s be clear: If our government takes the dark path, it will become the single most important battle over computational freedom of modern times. It is time for people to make a stand in defense of open source before it is too late. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m

Yes, LLM architectures are getting a little more complicated

The Kimi K3 architecture figure for yesterday's big open-weight model release, along with some observations and thoughts. 1. Yes, it looks relatively complicated, but it's essentially a scaled-up production version of their Kimi Linear model they released last year (scaled up from 48B -> 2.8T; K3 is by far the biggest open-weight model right now) 2. The one new component compared to Kimi Linear is the LatentMoE. I omitted it in the figure below since it's already very crowded, but that's essentially the same LatentMoE as in Nemotron 3 Ultra (you can find it in my LLM Architecture Gallery if you are curious). The idea here is to compress (down-project) large linear layers similar to multi-head latent attention. 3. Kimi K3's overall trend (similar to Nemotron 3, DeepSeek V4, and others) is also towards better inference efficiency. That is, there are many components that replace existing components with efficiency-tweaked versions. I.e., MoE -> LatentMoE, regular attention -> multi-head latent attention and Kimi Delta Attention. (I also have short tutorials and write-ups in my gallery if you are curious about additional details). 4. The one component change that is not an efficiency tweak is attention residuals. Like DeepSeek V4 improved the residual path with mHC (manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections), attention residuals are a way to improve the residual path, but it works a bit differently. I.e., mHC made the residual path wider. Attention residuals (also already part of Kimi Linear) connect the residuals across layers; the connection itself uses an attention score for an important/contribution weight. According to the report, it improves the validation loss and downstream performance (a bit) consistently and adds about 4% in training cost and 2% in inference cost. 5. Interestingly, Kimi K3 got rid of all RoPE layers and uses NoPE (No Positional Embeddings) everywhere instead. (Again, this is inherited from Kimi Linear). In other architectures, the recent trend was towards RoPE in local attention layers (like sliding window attention) and NoPE in the global layers. There were a few architectures that only used NoPE everywhere, but this is the first frontier-level one as far as I know. 6. Kimi K3 now also has native multimodal support, which is great! There are several other interesting training tidbits in the technical report, but that's it from the architecture front so far. A really great release overall.

great write up, evals are hard! here are 2 broad buckets we use to evaluate agents: 1. Measure the State of the World 2. Agent as a Judge on the Trajectory 1. Measure the state of the environment before and after the Agent does the Task. @harborframework and containerized Evals make this easier. The agent thinks in operating in a real world and we need to set up that world (files, installed tools, security boundaries, instructions) such that it mirrors what the agent will do in the real world. Every action the agent takes alters the world in some way. And success on a task means running a verification step on the final state of the world after the agent is done to see if this state corresponds to a successful pass. The tricky thing here is calibrating when the agent produces a final state that’s technically correct but your verifier didn’t forsee - you often want to allow this to pass or make sure the correct end state is capturable by your verifier. 2. Judge the trajectory -> Correctness is not the only factor - cost, latency, interpretability matter too. Those require understanding the action space The right answer is a good signal, but if the agent got there by cheating the Task then that means our agent is misaligned AND our task is bad because it allows cheating. If the agent is inefficient with cost/tokens, then that’s a signal that we may need to imbue more priors to help it find the correct trajectory (could be better prompting) we’ll be doing a bunch more educational content and open sourcing our tooling, reach out if there’s anything you want to see in particular! this should be accessible and easy for every team to do! Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch) Why is evaluating agents so difficult relative to evaluating a standard LLM? An LLM generates a single response to a prompt. An agent instead interacts with an environment by reasoning, calling tools, observing the results, and repeating. Rather than evaluating a single output, we are evaluating a full trajectory for a long horizon problem. Outcome & environment. Success is usually determined by the final outcome. Instead of checking the agent’s output, however, we usually check the actual state of the environment after a trajectory completes. For example: - A coding agent can say it fixed a bug but still fail test cases. - A personal assistant could say “your flight has been booked!”, but we don’t know if this is true until we check the booking database. The environment plays a huge role in the evaluation process. For example, we need a stable environment that does not change over time in order to run reliable evals, and we need this environment to be efficient so that evals can be run efficiently. Additionally, the environment must be realistic and expose the proper harness / tools for the agent to be effective. Environment state. The final answer is only one part of the evaluation. We also need to understand how the agent reached that answer. Did the agent use the correct tools? Did it interact efficiently with the environment? We can validate certain tool calls, check for intermediate solutions in the trajectory, and look at how many turns / tokens were used. Verifying intermediate trajectory states is common in agentic evaluation. If the agent solves a task, then this provides a valuable signal. But, what do we do if the agent solves a small ratio of tasks in a benchmark? In this case, we need to have a more granular measure of performance that allows us to understand how close the agent came to solving certain problems. Agent evals are expensive. Unlike traditional LLM benchmarks, agent evaluations can span long time horizons with many reasoning steps, tool calls, and environment interactions. A single evaluation may require vast amounts of generated tokens and dozens or hundreds of interaction turns with the environment. For this reason, agent evaluations are much more difficult to both curate and run! This data is super complex and even solving a single task can be expensive. Less data, more noise. Because each evaluation is costly, we typically run far fewer examples than in traditional LLM benchmarks. This is both because each task can take a long time to run and because curating the data / setup for each task is expensive. Rather than evaluating single dataset examples, we are asking the agent to solve a real problem. As a result, we usually have smaller evaluation dataset with higher variance, making reliable measurement difficult. — https://nitter.net/cwolferesearch/status/2083588813675274301#m

GPT-4 was the unlock for chat, Sonnet 3.5 was the unlock for code, and now Opus 4.5 is the unlock for agents. Thanks to Opus 4.5, agents can now work reliably on increasingly longer time horizons and get real-world work done on your behalf. Opus 4.5 is like a Waymo. You tell it "take me from A to B", and it takes you there. After a few of these experiences your brain realizes "oh. ok. we live in this world now". And then you're hooked. From that moment on, you'll never work the same way again. THE YEAR OF AGENTS 2025 has been touted as the year of agents, and Opus 4.5 + Claude Agent SDK is the pairing that makes that phrase true. With the SDK you get a world-class agentic harness out-of-the-box which you can now pair with Opus 4.5 to build real-world agents that actually work. I'm reminded of Alan Kay's quote "People who are really serious about software should make their own hardware". The agent version of this is "people who are serious about models should make their own harness". Anthropic clearly believes this, and it's working. The pairing of these tools is magic. I would describe myself as being "unhobblings-pilled", and the Claude Agent SDK + Opus 4.5 is the next major unhobbling. There's now another OOM of new latent economic value stuck in this combo, and it's the job of builders to get it out. If you were bearish on agents, now is the time to turn bullish. The open-model race is no longer about finding one universally “best” model. Apertus and @allen_ai 's OLMo optimize for transparency. @poolsideai 's Laguna and @Alibaba_Qwen optimize for hardware efficiency. @Macaron0fficial 's Macaron turns one base model into a set of swappable specialists. @Kimi_Moonshot 's K3, @deepseek_ai , @Zai_org 's GLM, and @MiniMax_AI push downloadable capability toward the closed frontier. That changes how you should compare them. > A model can be cheaper to run but harder to load > A model can be fully open but weaker on benchmarks > A model can be downloadable but impractical to host > A model can be modular but add routing failures One leaderboard cannot rank all four approaches well.

The better question is not “which open model is best?” It is “which trade-off fits the task?” We mapped the four camps and built a task-fit matrix for choosing between them. alphasignal.ai/news/the-open… Link The Open-Model Race has Split Four Ways | AlphaSignal Open-weight AI models now optimize for four distinct outcomes—deep transparency, hardware efficiency, modular specialization, or raw frontier capability—making alphasignal.ai

Your model router charges you for context that you've already paid for, eleven times over. Prompt caches belong to one model. Change the model during a session, and the new model will read everything all over again, at the full price. We priced it with three different session sizes. Same 12 turns, run five times. > One switch cost 11x warm > Routing somewhere else cost 47% more > Caches don't transfer between models Grok 4.5 gives output five times cheaper than the model it took over from. Price change was 0.2% in one test, and 7.9% in another. The second issue is hidden under all of that. Claude counts 58% more tokens than GPT for the same prompt. So, spending $2 instead of $5 is not a 60% savings. On the same prompt, it's closer to 37%. Which part owns the decision on which model to use?, When will a switch ever become profitable?, And why does it become even more expensive with longer runs?

processed.summary: Cette semaine a été riche en annonces et réflexions pour les débutants en IA ! Nous avons vu des modèles comme Astra d'OpenAI résoudre des problèmes mathématiques complexes, et Gemini Robotics 2 de Google DeepMind doter les robots d'une intelligence corporelle avancée. La conversation a également beaucoup tourné autour des 'agents IA' – ces systèmes capables de planifier et d'exécuter des tâches complexes, avec de nombreux exemples concrets d'utilisation. Enfin, un débat important sur l'accès aux modèles (ouverts vs fermés) et la sécurité de l'IA a animé les discussions.

glossaire.definition: Un modèle linguistique de grande taille est un programme d'IA entraîné sur d'énormes quantités de texte pour comprendre et générer du langage humain, comme ChatGPT ou Claude.
Un agent IA est un système capable de percevoir son environnement, de raisonner, de prendre des décisions et d'agir pour atteindre un objectif, souvent en utilisant des LLM et des outils externes.
Un modèle open-source est un modèle d'IA dont le code et/ou les 'poids' (les données internes apprises) sont librement accessibles et modifiables par tous, favorisant la transparence et l'innovation.
Un token est la plus petite unité de texte qu'un LLM traite (un mot, une partie de mot, un signe de ponctuation), et leur nombre influence souvent le coût et la vitesse d'utilisation du modèle.
Un prompt est l'instruction ou la question que vous donnez à un LLM pour qu'il génère une réponse, et bien le formuler est essentiel pour obtenir le résultat souhaité.
Un modèle multimodal peut comprendre et générer des informations à partir de plusieurs types de données, comme le texte, les images, le son ou la vidéo, pas seulement du texte.

Un 'harness' est un cadre logiciel ou un ensemble de réglages qui entoure un modèle d'IA pour le guider dans l'exécution de tâches complexes, lui permettant de mieux interagir avec l'environnement et les outils.

highlights.text_fr: On commence à quitter le territoire où l'on teste un LLM en lui disant par exemple "crée un SVG d'un pélican sur un vélo". Pour généraliser, je voulais savoir ce que ferait Opus 5 si je lui donnais le premier paragraphe du Seigneur des Anneaux, un budget de 1 million de tokens (environ 10$) et que je lui demandais un rendu 3D en javascript. Opus a travaillé environ 2 heures et a écrit 5500 lignes de code qui ont rendu (de manière procédurale) l'histoire. C'est un peu bancal mais amusant. C'est assez hallucinant que le LLM doive placer et orchestrer divers éléments polygonaux en coordonnées (x,y,z) et écrire du code qui anime le tout, et qu'il fasse même quelque chose du tout. J'aime aussi ce genre d'exemples car personne de sensé ne passerait jamais le temps d'écrire quelque chose d'aussi personnalisé, mais les LLM ont toute l'endurance et la patience du monde, c'est donc un exemple où l'on passe de "personne ne ferait jamais ça" à "bien sûr, pourquoi pas, c'est presque gratuit". Il pourrait y en avoir beaucoup plus. Mais je suis enthousiasmé par la création de mondes hyper-personnalisés dans lesquels on peut imaginer plonger des joueurs, par exemple pour participer à l'histoire du Seigneur des Anneaux en tant que PNJ spectateur, ou l'un des personnages, etc. Quelque chose comme un GTA éphémère de X à la demande. Une dernière pensée est que le domaine des mondes/jeux expose une faiblesse des LLM : ils ne peuvent pas facilement auditer leur travail car ils ne sont pas capables de percevoir efficacement et nativement des vidéos ou de jouer à des jeux. Ici, Opus 5 a dû prendre des captures d'écran très lentement et laborieusement à différents moments, et il a fait quelques erreurs et a créé pas mal de désordre. Un exemple de capacité brute (multimodale, gameplay) qui, je pense, manque encore beaucoup. Vidéo
highlights.text_original: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

highlights.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une bonne et longue session de "divagation". Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'adosser, passer en mode /voix et juste "divaguer" pendant environ 10 minutes, un désordre total, tout est permis, un flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare d'emblée, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale, désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, j'en fais une petite interview en quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont étonnamment bons pour reconstruire de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de votre propre enchevêtrement de pensées ressort beaucoup plus clair que ce avec quoi vous avez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la fusion mentale et que vous avez moins de choses à corriger à partir de ce moment-là.
highlights.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

actu.text_original: Thanks @ArtificialAnlys for working together on evaluations! Excited to see Inkling-small on the pareto line🫡 Artificial Analysis (@ArtificialAnlys) Thinking Machines' new Inkling Small scores 40 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, within a point of its flagship sibling Inkling with less than a third of the total and active parameters Inkling Small is @thinkymachines second model release, arriving two weeks after Inkling launched at 41 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. Thinking Machines is the San Francisco-based AI lab founded by former @OpenAI CTO Mira Murati. Inkling Small is an open weights reasoning model with 276B total parameters (12B active MoE), text, image, and speech input, and a 256K token context window. Key results: ➤ Inkling Small holds a similar tier of intelligence to Inkling’s at less than one third of its size: 276B total parameters (12B active) vs. 975B (41B active) for Inkling. No open weights model at its size or smaller scores higher on the Intelligence Index. DeepSeek V4 Flash (max), at a similar size of 284B total (13B active) also scores 40, MiniMax-M3 reaches 44 with 23B active, while GLM-5.2 (max) reaches 51 with 40B active. ➤ Inkling Small meets or exceeds Inkling on several coding and frontier reasoning evaluations. It scores higher on Humanity's Last Exam (32% vs. 30%), GPQA Diamond (89% vs. 87%), CritPt (8% vs. 5%), and SciCode (49% vs. 46%), and achieves the same score on Terminal Bench v2.1 (55%). ➤ Inkling Small is not as strong as Inkling on Agentic tasks and factual knowledge. Inkling Small trails Inkling on τ³-Banking (15% vs. 24%), though it edges ahead on GDPval-AA v2 (1269 vs. 1237 Elo). On the AA-Omniscience Index it scores -9 vs. the flagship's positive 2, meaning incorrect answers outweigh correct ones; this is driven by lower AA-Omniscience Accuracy (31% vs. 40%) rather than hallucination: Inkling Small’s Hallucination Rate is slightly lower than its larger sibling (57% vs. 63%). ➤ Inkling Small averaged ~24K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, slightly fewer than Inkling (~25K), while peers at its intelligence level averaged far more. DeepSeek V4 Flash averaged ~45K and GPT-5.4 mini (xhigh) ~78K. Running the full Intelligence Index took roughly the same number of output tokens for Inkling Small and Inkling. Additional model details: ➤ Type: Open weights reasoning model (Apache 2.0 license) ➤ Size: 276B total parameters, 12B active (MoE) ➤ Input modalities: Text, image, and speech ➤ Output modalities: Text ➤ Context window: 256K tokens (Inkling supports 1M) Congratulations to the team at Thinking Machines on the release! — https://nitter.net/ArtificialAnlys/status/2082894822180819057#m
actu.decryptage: La 'ligne de Pareto' représente l'équilibre optimal entre plusieurs critères, ici la performance et la taille d'un modèle. L''Intelligence Index' est un score qui mesure l'intelligence d'un modèle. 'Paramètres' sont les composants du modèle qui apprennent. 'MoE' (Mixture-of-Experts) est une architecture qui permet d'utiliser différents "experts" (parties du modèle) pour différentes tâches, améliorant l'efficacité. 'Fenêtre de contexte' est la quantité de texte que le modèle peut traiter en une seule fois. Les 'tâches Agentiques' sont des tâches nécessitant que l'IA planifie et exécute plusieurs étapes.

tips.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une bonne et longue session de "divagation". Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'adosser, passer en mode /voix et juste "divaguer" pendant environ 10 minutes, un désordre total, tout est permis, un flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare d'emblée, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale, désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, j'en fais une petite interview en quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont étonnamment bons pour reconstruire de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de votre propre enchevêtrement de pensées ressort beaucoup plus clair que ce avec quoi vous avez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la fusion mentale et que vous avez moins de choses à corriger à partir de ce moment-là.
tips.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

tips.text_fr: Super article, les évaluations sont difficiles ! Voici 2 grandes catégories que nous utilisons pour évaluer les agents : 1. Mesurer l'état du monde 2. L'agent comme juge sur la trajectoire 1. Mesurer l'état de l'environnement avant et après que l'agent ait effectué la tâche. @harborframework et les 'Evals' conteneurisés facilitent cela. L'agent pense en opérant dans un monde réel et nous devons configurer ce monde (fichiers, outils installés, limites de sécurité, instructions) de manière à ce qu'il reflète ce que l'agent fera dans le monde réel. Chaque action de l'agent modifie le monde d'une certaine manière. Et le succès d'une tâche signifie l'exécution d'une étape de vérification sur l'état final du monde une fois l'agent terminé pour voir si cet état correspond à un succès. Le point délicat ici est d'étalonner quand l'agent produit un état final qui est techniquement correct mais que votre vérificateur n'avait pas prévu - vous voulez souvent autoriser cela à passer ou vous assurer que l'état final correct est saisissable par votre vérificateur. 2. Juger la trajectoire -> La justesse n'est pas le seul facteur - le coût, la latence, l'interprétabilité comptent aussi. Ceux-ci nécessitent de comprendre l'espace d'action.
tips.text_original: great write up, evals are hard! here are 2 broad buckets we use to evaluate agents: 1. Measure the State of the World 2. Agent as a Judge on the Trajectory 1. Measure the state of the environment before and after the Agent does the Task. @harborframework and containerized Evals make this easier. The agent thinks in operating in a real world and we need to set up that world (files, installed tools, security boundaries, instructions) such that it mirrors what the agent will do in the real world. Every action the agent takes alters the world in some way. And success on a task means running a verification step on the final state of the world after the agent is done to see if this state corresponds to a successful pass. The tricky thing here is calibrating when the agent produces a final state that’s technically correct but your verifier didn’t forsee - you often want to allow this to pass or make sure the correct end state is capturable by your verifier. 2. Judge the trajectory -> Correctness is not the only factor - cost, latency, interpretability matter too. Those require understanding the action space The right answer is a good signal, but if the agent got there by cheating the Task then that means our agent is misaligned AND our task is bad because it allows cheating. If the agent is inefficient with cost/tokens, then that’s a signal that we may need to imbue more priors to help it find the correct trajectory (could be better prompting) we’ll be doing a bunch more educational content and open sourcing our tooling, reach out if there’s anything you want to see in particular! this should be accessible and easy for every team to do! Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch) Why is evaluating agents so difficult relative to evaluating a standard LLM? An LLM generates a single response to a prompt. An agent instead interacts with an environment by reasoning, calling tools, observing the results, and repeating. Rather than evaluating a single output, we are evaluating a full trajectory for a long horizon problem. Outcome & environment. Success is usually determined by the final outcome. Instead of checking the agent’s output, however, we usually check the actual state of the environment after a trajectory completes. For example: - A coding agent can say it fixed a bug but still fail test cases. - A personal assistant could say “your flight has been booked!”, but we don’t know if this is true until we check the booking database. The environment plays a huge role in the evaluation process. For example, we need a stable environment that does not change over time in order to run reliable evals, and we need this environment to be efficient so that evals can be run efficiently. Additionally, the environment must be realistic and expose the proper harness / tools for the agent to be effective. Environment state. The final answer is only one part of the evaluation. We also need to understand how the agent reached that answer. Did the agent use the correct tools? Did it interact efficiently with the environment? We can validate certain tool calls, check for intermediate solutions in the trajectory, and look at how many turns / tokens were used. Verifying intermediate trajectory states is common in agentic evaluation. If the agent solves a task, then this provides a valuable signal. But, what do we do if the agent solves a small ratio of tasks in a benchmark? In this case, we need to have a more granular measure of performance that allows us to understand how close the agent came to solving certain problems. Agent evals are expensive. Unlike traditional LLM benchmarks, agent evaluations can span long time horizons with many reasoning steps, tool calls, and environment interactions. A single evaluation may require vast amounts of generated tokens and dozens or hundreds of interaction turns with the environment. For this reason, agent evaluations are much more difficult to both curate and run! This data is super complex and even solving a single task can be expensive. Less data, more noise. Because each evaluation is costly, we typically run far fewer examples than in traditional LLM benchmarks. This is both because each task can take a long time to run and because curating the data / setup for each task is expensive. Rather than evaluating single dataset examples, we are asking the agent to solve a real problem. As a result, we usually have smaller evaluation dataset with higher variance, making reliable measurement difficult. — https://nitter.net/cwolferesearch/status/2083588813675274301#m

idees.text_fr: Ce n'est pas le moment de ralentir mais d'accélérer ! Les récentes cyberattaques alimentées par l'IA font parler tout le monde des risques de l'IA. Nous devrions. Pour y arriver, nous avons besoin de trois choses à mon avis : - Accroître la transparence avec un partage de traces obligatoire et la divulgation d'incidents pour les cyberattaques d'agents - Maintenir l'illégalité des cyberattaques alimentées par l'IA, avec des sanctions significatives pour les décourager - Équiper les défenseurs de la meilleure IA, en particulier des modèles ouverts, pour réduire l'asymétrie des capacités entre les attaquants et les défenseurs. idees.text_original: It's not time to slow down but to accelerate! The recent AI-powered cyberattacks have everyone talking about the risks of AI. We should. But let's not lose sight of the bigger picture! If we work hard at it, AI will make the world safer, not less safe, just as most major technologies have. We've already seen a glimpse of that: we defended ourselves with AI (more specifically an open model). The same systems that helped stop an AI-powered cyberattack can now help defend against millions of cyberattacks every day, while helping us identify and fix vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them. To get there, we need three things in my opinion: - Increase transparency with mandatory trace sharing and incident disclosure for agent cyber-attacks - Keep AI-powered cyberattacks illegal, with meaningful penalties to disincentivize them - Equip defenders with the best AI, especially open models, to reduce the asymmetry of capabilities between attackers and defenders If we get those three things right, AI won't just create new cybersecurity challenges, it will make cybersecurity fundamentally and meaningfully stronger. And that's before considering AI's impact on science, healthcare, education, productivity, and much more. It's not time to slow down but to accelerate!

idees.text_fr: Pour aborder les limites du "deep learning" et éviter de stagner, le domaine de l'IA a commencé par appliquer le patch (1), qui a commencé à être démontré 9 mois plus tard en décembre 2024 et est maintenant devenu complètement omniprésent. idees.text_original: To address the limits of deep learning and avoid stalling, the field of AI started by applying patch (1), which started being demoed 9 months later in December 2024 and has now become completely ubiquitous. However, long term, it is simply inevitable that AI will move to patch (2). François Chollet (@fchollet) There are essentially two main options to remedy this: 1. Find ways to perform active inference, so that the model adapts its learned program in contact with a new data distribution at test time. Would likely lead to some meaningful progress, but it isn't the ultimate solution, more of an incremental improvement. 2. Change the training mechanism to something more robust than SGD, such as the MDL principle. This would pretty much require moving away from deep learning (curve fitting) altogether and embracing discrete program search instead (which I have advocated for many years as a way to tackle reasoning problems...) — https://nitter.net/fchollet/status/1766044732830999014#m

idees.text_fr: Je sais qu'il est très tentant de se moquer, et c'est juste, mais pour être clair, ma critique passée des LLM de base ne s'applique pas aux systèmes TTA, de la même manière que la critique des limites des trains à vapeur ne s'appliquerait pas aux trains à grande vitesse électrifiés d'aujourd'hui (même s'ils semblent similaires et utilisent la même plateforme, les principes en jeu sont substantiellement différents). François Chollet explique que ses critiques passées concernent les LLM sans ces améliorations, et non les systèmes plus sophistiqués intégrant le TTA.

idees.text_fr: Petit rappel de ce qui est acceptable ou non avec les "harnesses" utilisés pour jouer à ARC-AGI-3 : 1. Par le passé, nous avons eu beaucoup d'échanges avec OpenAI sur la meilleure façon de tester leurs modèles, notamment en ce qui concerne la compression. Je suis content qu'ils commencent à trouver la réponse. Bien sûr, si chaque fournisseur utilise des paramètres différents lors du test de son modèle, cela crée un problème de parité potentiel. My take is that this is fine as long as the settings and the cost are clearly reported.

Le tweet discute de la bonne manière de tester les modèles, en évitant les "harnesses" qui trichent en ayant des connaissances spécifiques sur les tests, et en assurant la "parité" (comparabilité) des résultats entre les différents fournisseurs d'IA.

idees.text_fr: Il y a quinze ans, @Coursera et les cours en ligne ont changé l'éducation. Cela a mieux fonctionné que presque tout le monde ne l'avait prévu, élargissant l'accès en ouvrant les lieux d'apprentissage. Mais la manière d'apprendre reste largement la même depuis des siècles : c'est toujours un modèle unique, enseigné de la même manière à chaque personne qui se présente. Nous avons maintenant l'occasion de changer la manière dont l'apprentissage se déroule. Grâce aux avancées de l'IA, nous pouvons désormais construire un guide d'apprentissage personnalisé pour chaque personne. Nous transformerons l'apprentissage d'un modèle un-à-plusieurs à un modèle un-à-un. Je lance LearnVector pour inventer cette prochaine génération d'apprentissage.
idees.text_original: Fifteen years ago, @Coursera and online courses changed education. It worked better than almost anyone expected, expanding access by opening up where you can learn. But how you learn remains largely the same as it has for centuries: it is still one-size-fits-all, taught the same way to each person who shows up. We now have an opportunity to change how learning happens. With advances in AI, we can now build a custom learning guide for each person. We will turn learning from one‑to‑many to one‑to‑one. I'm starting LearnVector to invent this next generation of learning. We are starting with a $100M investment from Coursera, and plan to collaborate closely with Coursera and Udemy. Good learning needs much more than just a chatbot. Research shows that chatbots without guardrails harm learning. They help complete tasks and enable students to do better on homework. But cognitive offloading to a chatbot results in them being less skilled. And, you cannot always trust what a chatbot tells you. In contrast, LearnVector will plan a path with you, adapt to how you learn, and patiently stay with you until you’ve mastered new skills. One thing has not changed in all this time. People want learning they can trust: material that is accurate, relevant, and worth the effort you put into it. Anything less wastes the most valuable thing a learner has: time. Coursera has a trusted library of materials from authoritative sources. LearnVector plans to work with Coursera to bring this trustworthy learning to everyone. I'm grateful to Greg Hart and the entire Coursera team for supporting LearnVector. I look forward to working with our talented team to change how we learn, and accelerate human development. learnvector.ai
idees.decryptage: Ce tweet présente "LearnVector", une nouvelle initiative qui vise à transformer l'éducation en utilisant l'IA pour créer des expériences d'apprentissage "un-à-un" (personnalisées pour chaque élève), contrairement au modèle traditionnel "un-à-plusieurs". Il souligne l'importance d'un apprentissage fiable, au-delà des simples "chatbots".

idees.text_fr: Adam Thierer avait écrit le livre marquant sur l'"innovation sans permission". Nous obtenons les meilleures idées lorsque nous n'avons pas à demander l'autorisation au gouvernement à l'avance pour inventer. Protéger l'IA open source est désormais un élément essentiel pour garantir cela.
idees.text_original: Adam Thierer had written the landmark book on "Permissionless Innovation." We get the best ideas when we don't have to ask the government in advance for permission to invent. Protecting open source AI is now a critical part of ensuring this. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) We stand at a critical crossroads in the debate over AI governance in the United States, and it feels like we are inching closer to a very serious battle over whether or not open source models will even be allowed in an environment where a new de facto licensing regime has been taking shape. Lacking formal congressional statutory frameworks or clear administration rules (like the diffusion rule revision), we appear to be left with a sporadic, arbitrary, non-transparent process for model review. The fiction of “voluntary” agreements hangs over this debate, and some large model developers are already showing an incredible willingness to bend over backwards to accommodate national security-related officials / orders that the rest of us are not privy to. It's a very opaque process. And those model developers are expected to play ball with those officials, or else their models get pulled from the market or held up for long periods. Or they will lose any government procurement contracts they have. There is nothing “voluntary” about it when that Sword of Damocles hangs in the room. As this mess worsens, at some point the question of how to handle open source models will come into sharper focus because it will have to. I've even heard some rumors lately that something may be coming from the admin on this front to address this. Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. If that happens, then we would be right back in the thick of a Clipper Chip-like battle along the lines of what we saw in the late 1990s. That is a much darker path for America. Meanwhile, open source developers have no “golden shares” or other goodies to offer the government to make their problems go away. Let’s be clear: If our government takes the dark path, it will become the single most important battle over computational freedom of modern times. It is time for people to make a stand in defense of open source before it is too late.

idees.text_fr: La figure de l'architecture Kimi K3 pour la grande version du modèle open-weight d'hier, avec quelques observations et réflexions. 1. Oui, cela semble relativement compliqué, mais c'est essentiellement une version de production "à l'échelle" de leur modèle Kimi Linear qu'ils ont sorti l'année dernière (passé de 48B -> 2.8T ; K3 est de loin le plus grand modèle open-weight à l'heure actuelle) 2. Le seul nouveau composant par rapport à Kimi Linear est le LatentMoE. Je l'ai omis dans la figure ci-dessous car elle est déjà très chargée, mais c'est essentiellement le même LatentMoE que dans Nemotron 3 Ultra. L'idée ici est de compresser (projeter vers le bas) de grandes couches linéaires, de manière similaire à l'attention latente multi-têtes. 3. La tendance générale de Kimi K3 (similaire à Nemotron 3, DeepSeek V4 et autres) est également vers une meilleure efficacité d'inférence. C'est-à-dire qu'il existe de nombreux composants qui remplacent les composants existants par des versions optimisées en termes d'efficacité. I.e., MoE -> LatentMoE, attention régulière -> attention latente multi-têtes et Kimi Delta Attention. 4. Le seul changement de composant qui n'est pas une optimisation d'efficacité est celui des résidus d'attention. Comme DeepSeek V4 a amélioré le chemin résiduel avec mHC (Hyper-Connexions à contrainte de manifold), les résidus d'attention sont un moyen d'améliorer le chemin résiduel, mais cela fonctionne un peu différemment. I.e., mHC a élargi le chemin résiduel. Les résidus d'attention (également déjà présents dans Kimi Linear) connectent les résidus à travers les couches ; la connexion elle-même utilise un score d'attention pour un poids important/contribution. Selon le rapport, cela améliore la perte de validation et les performances en aval (un peu) de manière constante et ajoute environ 4% en coût d'entraînement et 2% en coût d'inférence. 5. Fait intéressant, Kimi K3 s'est débarrassé de toutes les couches RoPE et utilise NoPE (No Positional Embeddings) partout à la place. (Encore une fois, ceci est hérité de Kimi Linear). Dans d'autres architectures, la tendance récente était vers RoPE dans les couches d'attention locales (comme l'attention par fenêtre glissante) et NoPE dans les couches globales. Il y avait quelques architectures qui n'utilisaient que NoPE partout, mais c'est la première de niveau "frontier" à ma connaissance. 6. Kimi K3 a maintenant également un support multimodal natif, ce qui est excellent ! Il y a plusieurs autres détails d'entraînement intéressants dans le rapport technique, mais c'est tout pour l'architecture jusqu'à présent. Une très bonne publication dans l'ensemble.
idees.text_original: The Kimi K3 architecture figure for yesterday's big open-weight model release, along with some observations and thoughts. 1. Yes, it looks relatively complicated, but it's essentially a scaled-up production version of their Kimi Linear model they released last year (scaled up from 48B -> 2.8T; K3 is by far the biggest open-weight model right now) 2. The one new component compared to Kimi Linear is the LatentMoE. I omitted it in the figure below since it's already very crowded, but that's essentially the same LatentMoE as in Nemotron 3 Ultra (you can find it in my LLM Architecture Gallery if you are curious). The idea here is to compress (down-project) large linear layers similar to multi-head latent attention. 3. Kimi K3's overall trend (similar to Nemotron 3, DeepSeek V4, and others) is also towards better inference efficiency. That is, there are many components that replace existing components with efficiency-tweaked versions. I.e., MoE -> LatentMoE, regular attention -> multi-head latent attention and Kimi Delta Attention. (I also have short tutorials and write-ups in my gallery if you are curious about additional details). 4. The one component change that is not an efficiency tweak is attention residuals. Like DeepSeek V4 improved the residual path with mHC (manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections), attention residuals are a way to improve the residual path, but it works a bit differently. I.e., mHC made the residual path wider. Attention residuals (also already part of Kimi Linear) connect the residuals across layers; the connection itself uses an attention score for an important/contribution weight. According to the report, it improves the validation loss and downstream performance (a bit) consistently and adds about 4% in training cost and 2% in inference cost. 5. Interestingly, Kimi K3 got rid of all RoPE layers and uses NoPE (No Positional Embeddings) everywhere instead. (Again, this is inherited from Kimi Linear). In other architectures, the recent trend was towards RoPE in local attention layers (like sliding window attention) and NoPE in the global layers. There were a few architectures that only used NoPE everywhere, but this is the first frontier-level one as far as I know. 6. Kimi K3 now also has native multimodal support, which is great! There are several other interesting training tidbits in the technical report, but that's it from the architecture front so far. A really great release overall.

Decentralization creates checks and balances on power. By contrast, centralized alternatives, like bureaucratic approval regimes and mandatory gatekeeping, typically produce regulatory capture and reinforce cartels. outils.text_fr: On commence à quitter le territoire où l'on teste un LLM en lui disant par exemple "crée un SVG d'un pélican sur un vélo". Pour généraliser, je voulais savoir ce que ferait Opus 5 si je lui donnais le premier paragraphe du Seigneur des Anneaux, un budget de 1 million de tokens (environ 10$) et que je lui demandais un rendu 3D en javascript. Opus a travaillé environ 2 heures et a écrit 5500 lignes de code qui ont rendu (de manière procédurale) l'histoire. C'est un peu bancal mais amusant. C'est assez hallucinant que le LLM doive placer et orchestrer divers éléments polygonaux en coordonnées (x,y,z) et écrire du code qui anime le tout, et qu'il fasse même quelque chose du tout. J'aime aussi ce genre d'exemples car personne de sensé ne passerait jamais le temps d'écrire quelque chose d'aussi personnalisé, mais les LLM ont toute l'endurance et la patience du monde, c'est donc un exemple où l'on passe de "personne ne ferait jamais ça" à "bien sûr, pourquoi pas, c'est presque gratuit". Il pourrait y en avoir beaucoup plus. Mais je suis enthousiasmé par la création de mondes hyper-personnalisés dans lesquels on peut imaginer plonger des joueurs, par exemple pour participer à l'histoire du Seigneur des Anneaux en tant que PNJ spectateur, ou l'un des personnages, etc. Quelque chose comme un GTA éphémère de X à la demande. Une dernière pensée est que le domaine des mondes/jeux expose une faiblesse des LLM : ils ne peuvent pas facilement auditer leur travail car ils ne sont pas capables de percevoir efficacement et nativement des vidéos ou de jouer à des jeux. Ici, Opus 5 a dû prendre des captures d'écran très lentement et laborieusement à différents moments, et il a fait quelques erreurs et a créé pas mal de désordre. Un exemple de capacité brute (multimodale, gameplay) qui, je pense, manque encore beaucoup. Vidéo
outils.text_original: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video
